title: Settle a Falling-Candy Board
statement:
A match-three game stores its board as a grid board. A positive number is a candy of that colour; 0 is an empty cell. Empty cells always sit above every candy in their column.

The game settles the board by repeating these steps until nothing changes:

  1. Mark every candy that is part of a horizontal or vertical line of three or more adjacent candies of the same colour. Mark all such lines first, before removing anything; one candy may belong to a row line and a column line at once.
  2. Crush: every marked cell becomes empty.
  3. Drop: in each column, candies fall straight down to fill the empty cells below them, keeping their order. Empty cells end up at the top.

When a mark step finds no line, the board is stable. Return the stable board.

examples.why: The left column is a vertical line of three 1s. Nothing sits above it, so after crushing, the column is simply empty.
Crushing the three 3s drops the 5 to the bottom row, where it now lines up with the two other 5s. A second round crushes that row. Stopping after one round is wrong.
The top row and the middle column cross at a shared 3. Both lines are marked before anything is removed. Crushing the row first would leave only two 3s in the column.

constraints: empty cells are above all candies in their column
hints: Split one round into three separate passes: find every line, clear the marked cells, then let each column fall.
Mark into a separate boolean grid (or flip marked values negative) so that clearing one line cannot hide another line that crosses it.
For the drop, walk each column from the bottom with a write pointer: copy every candy down to the pointer, then fill the rest of the column with 0. Repeat rounds until a mark pass finds nothing.

explain.intuition:
This is a simulation, so the work is in doing the steps in the right order. The key rule is that marking is simultaneous: find all lines on the current board before changing any cell. If you remove a row line right away, a column line that shares a candy with it may drop to two candies and survive, which is the third example. A separate "marked" grid, or making marked values negative while still comparing absolute values, keeps the board readable while you mark.

Dropping is the "move the zeros to one end" trick, once per column. Walk from the bottom up with a write pointer; each surviving candy is copied to the pointer, which then moves up. Everything above the pointer becomes empty. Then go back to marking, because candies that fell may now line up (second example). Stop when a mark pass finds nothing.
steps: Mark: for every cell, if it and the next two to the right are the same non-zero colour, mark all three; do the same for the next two below.
If nothing was marked, return the board.
Crush: set every marked cell to 0.
Drop: for each column, walk from the bottom row up with a write row w; copy each non-zero value to row w and move w up; then set rows w and above to 0.
Go back to the mark step.
pitfalls: Crushing each line as soon as you find it, so crossing lines lose their shared candy before they are counted.
Running only one round. Falling candies can form new lines.
Treating three empty cells in a row as a line. Only non-zero values can match.

complexity.time: O((r·c)²) in the worst case: each round is O(r·c) and removes at least 3 candies

solutions.title: Mark grid, crush, drop
solutions.idea: Each round marks every line in a boolean grid, clears the marked cells, and compacts each column downward.

solutions.title: Mark by flipping the sign
solutions.idea: Mark a candy by making it negative, and compare absolute values so marked candies still form lines with their neighbours. No extra grid.

followups: Score the result: each crushed candy is worth points, multiplied by the round number of its chain. What do you track?
Only lines touching the cells that moved last round can be new. How would you avoid rescanning the whole board each round?
